synopsis: ISO/TS 21815-2:2021, edition 1, was published on 14 July 2021 and confirmed in December 2024; it defines the on-board J1939 collision-avoidance interface, including slow-down, controlled-stop, emergency-stop and motion-inhibit commands, capability discovery and keep-alive messaging [f2156, f2057, f3638, f12979]. The interface anchors the booklet’s brake-request contract and offers a precedent for reusing evidence across machine models, but is explicitly not plug-and-play: machine and collision-system manufacturers must agree integration details and demonstrate interoperability [f13229, f367, f2159, f10726]. SIL cannot establish unexpected CAN/J1939 timing behaviour, whereas HIL can test real controller, bus and I/O timing; validation through a third-party J1939 interface must include end-to-end integration latency [f530, f931, f8198]. A production-relevant HIL bench could target mid-2027, but should not become critical-path work unless ECU, bus and actuator interfaces stabilise early; unanalysed interface or controller changes in 2027 may invalidate the pre-built simulator [f857, f11028]. Record machine-network state, brake requests and measured responses with adequate rate and precision, preserving DBC/message-schema versions and exact hardware/software provenance so behaviour can be reconstructed [f5634, f12982, f5646, f12992]. Spoofed or stale messages, bus faults and incompatible implementations must not cause unsafe brake commands, and explicit fault testing is required; nevertheless, J1939 cybersecurity was omitted from the machine-motion questions and needs separate treatment because ISO 19014-4 excludes it [f2936, f8200, f6607, f5832].

relations.note: Provides the exact publication date and edition for the July 2021 standard.
Dates confirmation of the published J1939 interface specification to December 2024.
Both define slow, stop and motion-prevention commands; the latter specifies standstill.
Both identify ISO/TS 21815-2:2021 as the J1939 braking interface framework.
Both anchor the brake request in the ISO/TS 21815-2 J1939 interface.
Both reject plug-and-play implementation and require additional integration agreements.
Both explicitly state that the device-to-machine interface is not plug-and-play.
Repeat the three stop/slow commands, capability discovery and keep-alive messaging.
Both require end-to-end integration-latency validation when intervention uses J1939.
Both prohibit unsafe brake commands from spoofing, stale messages, faults or incompatible implementations.
Both state that HIL can emulate the standardized J1939 intervention interface.
Both flag unanalysed 2027 prototype-interface changes as simulator-validity risks.
SIL timing limitations motivate using the real J1939 intervention interface in HIL.
HIL measures real bus and controller timing needed for integration-latency validation.
Adds DBC and message-schema version recording to the machine-state logging requirements.
Extends interface-version provenance to binaries, firmware, configurations, checksums and logging software.
Cybersecurity's exclusion from ISO 19014-4 motivates separate brake-network security treatment.
Dependence on stable interfaces explains why unanalysed changes threaten a pre-built simulator.
